analysis.one_liner: Taxes opioid painkiller makers one cent per milligram to fund addiction treatment, with rebates for cancer and hospice patients.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee in February 2019 and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would charge opioid manufacturers, producers, and importers a fee of one cent per milligram on the opioid painkillers they sell. It exempts drugs used to treat opioid addiction, and it requires the Health and Human Services Department to rebate or discount the fee for cancer and hospice patients so they pay nothing extra. Every dollar of revenue left over after those rebates would go to states, locked to spending on substance abuse treatment: new treatment facilities, sober living housing, care for babies born in withdrawal, and recruiting treatment workers in rural and underserved areas.
analysis.who_benefits: People with opioid addiction who need treatment, especially in rural and underserved communities where treatment facilities and providers are scarce; families affected by addiction; and babies born with neonatal abstinence syndrome. Cancer and hospice patients who legitimately need opioids are specifically protected from the fee through mandatory rebates or discounts.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People needing addiction treatment, especially in underserved areas

how_it_helps.text: Imposes a one-cent-per-milligram fee on active opioids sold by manufacturers, producers, or importers, producing revenue dedicated to treatment [S2][S3].

Requires states to spend the resulting revenue exclusively on substance abuse treatment: new residential and outpatient facilities, sober living housing, long-term 30-, 60-, and 90-day treatment programs, housing for children of parents in treatment, facilities for babies with neonatal abstinence syndrome, and support services like employment and housing for people in recovery [S2][S3].
Directs some funding to recruit and train substance use disorder professionals to work in rural and medically underserved communities [S2][S3].
Requires HHS to rebate or discount the fee for cancer and hospice patients so they face no economic burden from it, shielding legitimate pain patients [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Opioid manufacturers, producers, and importers, who would pay the fee on every milligram of active opioid they sell. Some of that cost could be passed through to retail prices for patients outside the cancer and hospice rebate program.

drawbacks.text: The fee is charged per milligram regardless of the drug's price, so it falls hardest on inexpensive generic opioids; a common 10-milligram tablet would carry a 10-cent fee, a large multiple of the pill's manufacturing cost. That could raise retail prices for patients with chronic pain who are not covered by the cancer and hospice rebate [S3].

The bill relies on HHS to build a rebate and discount program quickly enough that cancer and hospice patients never feel the fee; any lag or gap in that mechanism would briefly leave vulnerable patients paying more until rebates arrive [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The trade is straightforward: a per-milligram fee on the companies that make opioid painkillers funds addiction treatment, with the patients most likely to need opioids for legitimate reasons (cancer and hospice care) explicitly shielded. The main honest concern is that pain patients outside the rebate program could face higher prices, and the fee structure is crude because it taxes volume rather than price. But the money is locked to treatment uses by law, and the bill includes its own oversight report to Congress on retail prices and patient access [S2][S3].

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Finance Committee on the day it was introduced, and the committee never took it up, so it died there when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Joe Manchin introduced the bill on February 7, 2019, joined by nine cosponsors (eight Democrats and one Independent) [S3][S4].
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance, which has jurisdiction over tax bills [S5].
No further action was ever taken: no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor vote, and the bill died at the end of the 116th Congress [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Opioid manufacturers are better off: the fee was never imposed and no dedicated treatment funding stream was created. Nothing in the record shows any hearing or committee action on the bill after referral.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Opioid manufacturers, who never paid the fee

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all nine cosponsors were Democrats and one Independent; no Republican cosponsored, and the Republican-run Finance Committee and Senate majority took no action on it.

industries.note: The bill would put a one-cent-per-milligram fee on every active opioid they sell, with revenue locked to addiction treatment. The fee was never imposed, so the companies avoided a new cost tied to the products at the center of the overdose crisis.
Because the fee is per milligram rather than a percentage of price, it is proportionally largest on cheap generic opioids, the segment with the thinnest margins.

industries.industry: Drugs for opioid addiction treatment (e.g., buprenorphine, methadone makers)
industries.note: Medications used exclusively to treat opioid addiction are explicitly excluded from the fee, and state treatment funding would expand the market for medication-assisted treatment.
